blocks.text: A **stack** is a collection where you can only add or remove items at **one end**, called the **top**. The last item you put in is always the first one you take out. That rule has a name: **LIFO** — **last in, first out**.

blocks.alt: A stack of four plates. A new plate is pushed onto the top, and the only plate that can be taken off is the top one. The plates underneath can't be reached without removing the ones above them.
blocks.caption: Only the top is ever touched.

blocks.text: Think of a stack of plates

In a cafeteria, clean plates are stacked on top of each other. You put a clean plate **on top**, and you take the plate **from the top**. Nobody pulls a plate out of the middle. A stack in programming follows exactly the same rules:

items: **push** — put a new item on top.
**pop** — take the top item off (and get it back).
**peek** (also called **top**) — look at the top item without removing it.
**isEmpty** — are there any items at all?

blocks.text: Every one of these is **O(1)**: none of them ever has to look past the top item, no matter how tall the stack gets.
Last in, first out
Watch the order things come out. Push 10, 20 and 30, then pop: you get **30** back — the last one in. Push order and pop order are always **reversed**.

blocks.alt: Five snapshots of one stack. Start empty. Push 10. Push 20. Push 30, so 30 is on top. Pop returns 30 and leaves 10 and 20, with 20 now on top. Peek returns 20 and changes nothing.

blocks.text: Try your own sequence. Notice that pop always takes whatever went in **most recently**.

blocks.caption: Type operations like push 5, pop, peek, size — then step through them.

Each language reports an empty pop its own way — `undefined`, `None`, `null` or an exception — but the idea is the same: there was nothing to take.
Stack or queue?

A **queue** is the stack's twin with the opposite rule: items join at the **back** and leave from the **front**, like people in a line — **first in, first out** (FIFO). Same items, same order in, opposite order out:

blocks.alt: Left: a stack with 1, 2, 3 pushed in that order; the item that leaves first is 3, from the top. Right: a queue with 1, 2, 3 joined in that order; the item that leaves first is 1, from the front.

blocks.text: Choosing between them is usually the first decision in a problem: does the **newest** item matter most (stack), or the **oldest** (queue)?
Underflow and overflow
Two things can go wrong, and both have names you'll hear in interviews:

blocks.alt: Left: an empty stack; calling pop has nothing to remove, which is a stack underflow. Right: a stack with a fixed capacity of three that is already full; pushing one more item has nowhere to go, which is a stack overflow.

items: **Stack underflow** — calling pop or peek on an **empty** stack. Always check `isEmpty()` first when the stack might be empty.

**Stack overflow** — pushing onto a stack that is **full**. This happens with fixed-size arrays, and with the program's own call stack when recursion never stops (that's where the website Stack Overflow got its name).

blocks.text: One idea, two ways to build it
"Stack" describes **behaviour** — push, pop, peek — not how the items are stored. That makes it an **abstract data type**. The two classic ways to build one:

blocks.alt: Left: an array holding 5, 8, 3 with an index called top pointing at the last used slot, index 2; push writes at index 3. Right: a linked list 3 to 8 to 5 to null where the head is the top of the stack; push adds a new node in front of the head.

Words you'll see everywhere

blocks.alt: A glossary: top is the item that was added last; push adds on top; pop removes from the top; peek reads the top without removing it; LIFO means last in, first out; underflow is popping an empty stack; overflow is pushing onto a full one.

elements.text:
top        the item added most recently
push(x)    add x on top
pop()      remove the top and return it
peek()     read the top, leave it there
LIFO       last in, first out
underflow  pop or peek on an empty stack
overflow   push onto a full stack

blocks.text: Key takeaways

items: A stack only lets you touch the **top**: push on, pop off, peek at it.
Items come out in the **reverse** of the order they went in — **LIFO**.
push, pop, peek, isEmpty and size are all **O(1)**.
Popping an empty stack is **underflow**; pushing onto a full one is **overflow**.
A stack is a behaviour, not a storage layout — you can build it on an **array** or a **linked list**.
